transcript.text:
This could be something simple such as the child lock, hob isolator or a tripped breaker, but the likely fault depends on whether it is induction, glass ceramic or solid-plate, and whether one zone or every zone is affected. 1. Check the wall/cupboard hob isolator is on, and look at the consumer unit for a tripped breaker. If a breaker trips again, leave it off and arrange an electrician or appliance engineer rather than repeatedly resetting it.
2. If it has touch controls, look for a key or padlock symbol and try the normal unlock procedure shown on the control panel/manual. A lock can prevent zones starting.
3. If it is induction, try a flat magnetic pan that works on another zone. If that pan works, the original pan is unsuitable; if it does not, the zone itself may have a fault. Is it an induction hob (it needs magnetic pans), a smooth glass ceramic hob, or solid electric plates — and are all zones affected or only one?
It's a smooth glass ceramic one, a Zanussi. Only the rear right zone isn't working, the other three are fine. Display shows the power number for it though.

Because the other three zones work and the display accepts a power setting for the rear-right one, the controls are at least registering your selection. The most likely cause is a failed radiant heating element for that zone, or its control switch/regulator; a loose or heat-damaged connection underneath is another possibility. 1. Check the hob isolator and its consumer-unit breaker are on. A supply fault is less likely with three working zones, but if a breaker has tripped or trips again, leave it off and arrange an engineer/electrician.
2. With the glass cool and dry, put a pan on the rear-right zone, set it to full power briefly, and carefully check whether the pan/surface warms at all. If it stays cold despite the display showing a setting, that points to the zone element, its control, or its wiring rather than a setting issue. If the glass is cracked or chipped, stop using the hob until it is repaired. Otherwise, a single dead ceramic zone normally needs an appliance engineer to test the element and connections with the hob isolated; it is not usually an owner-safe repair because access involves mains wiring and dismantling the hob.
I tried it on full and it stays cold, no red glow at all and nothing warms up. No tripped breaker, the other zones are fine. It was slow to boil for a while before it stopped, if that helps.

The most likely fault is the rear-right radiant heating element. A zone becoming progressively slow to boil and then going completely cold, with no red glow, is a typical element failure. The fact that its display still accepts a power setting and the other three zones work makes a whole-hob supply or control-lock problem very unlikely. The other possibilities are that zone’s energy regulator/control, or a burnt/loose connection beneath the hob. An engineer can confirm which by isolating the hob, removing it safely, and testing the element and its connections. There is no further useful owner-safe check here: access involves mains wiring and lifting/dismantling the glass hob. Arrange a cooker/appliance engineer, and describe it as: “Zanussi glass ceramic hob; rear-right radiant zone had become slow, now has no heat or red glow although the display shows a power setting.” You can continue using the other zones if the glass is intact and there is no burning smell, crack, sparking or erratic behaviour. If any of those occur, switch the hob off at its isolator and stop using it.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that.
